notes: All english fields equal the SOV 1970 focus tree party names. Slot 1 keeps abbr null because the tree name already contains '(NTS)' (avoids '(NTS) - People's Labour Union (NTS)'). Slot 2: the Committee for Human Rights was formally constituted on 4 Nov 1970; the text presents Sakharov's rights-defender circle as of Jan 1970. Slot 14 uses Solzhenitsyn's creed as label (the essay itself dates from 1974). Slots 8-11 are the tree's invented clandestine bodies, rooted in real Shia, Bukharan emigre and Basmachi milieus. Icons: CPSU = SOV_kpss, Council of Marshals = SOV_comm_military_junta (MD Armed Forces of the Soviet Union), House of Romanov = SOV_nationalist_monarchist.

0.name: Sistemnoye upravleniye
0.text:
The Systems Directorate is the informal network of 'systems men' around Dzhermen Gvishiani, deputy chairman of the State Committee for Science and Technology since 1965 and son-in-law of Premier Alexei Kosygin. Gvishiani manages licence deals and scientific exchanges with the capitalist world and has been negotiating with McGeorge Bundy since 1967 over a joint East-West institute for applied systems analysis.

Its creed is management, not ideology: cybernetics, computers, imported Western plants such as the Fiat works rising at Togliatti, and rule by trained executives under a firm authoritarian hand. It wants detente, credits and technology from the West while keeping the one-party order intact. Its leverage lies in Kosygin's government, the research institutes and the foreign trade apparatus.

1.name: Narodno-trudovoy soyuz rossiyskikh solidaristov
1.text:
The People's Labour Union is the most active Russian émigré organization of the Cold War. Founded in Belgrade in 1930 by young émigrés, it works from Frankfurt am Main, where its Posev publishing house prints the journals Posev and Grani for smuggling into the USSR. Its chairman since 1955 is Vladimir Poremsky, theorist of a 'molecular' revolution built from small, unconnected cells inside the country.

Its ideology is solidarism: a Christian, anti-Marxist order of private property, cooperation between classes, local self-government and a law-bound Russian state. Firmly pro-Western, it relies on couriers, radio broadcasts and contacts with dissidents, but the KGB has penetrated its networks and Soviet courts use its name to brand opponents as traitors.

2.name: Komitet prav cheloveka
2.text:
The Committee for Human Rights is the organizing core of the Soviet rights defenders, built around Andrei Sakharov, father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb. Barred from secret work since his 1968 essay 'Reflections on Progress, Peaceful Coexistence and Intellectual Freedom' appeared in the West, Sakharov is moving into open dissent alongside Valery Chalidze and Andrei Tverdokhlebov, while the samizdat Chronicle of Current Events documents arrests and trials.

Its weapon is the Soviet constitution itself: freedom of speech and conscience, public trials, an end to psychiatric repression and the right to emigrate. Sakharov's call for convergence of socialism and capitalism, disarmament and cooperation with the West wins admiration abroad. At home its leverage is moral authority, samizdat and foreign radio.

3.name: Soyuz demokraticheskikh sotsialistov
3.text:
The Union of Democratic Socialists unites the 'party democrats' of the Soviet intelligentsia: Marxists who believe the revolution was betrayed by Stalin, not by Lenin. Its leading figure is the historian Roy Medvedev, expelled from the CPSU in 1969 over his manuscript history of Stalinism, 'Let History Judge', and editor of the samizdat Political Diary. His twin brother Zhores, the biologist who exposed Lysenko, shares his cause.

They want socialist democracy rather than capitalism: competing candidates, freedom of the press and of science, the full truth about the purges and the spirit of the Prague Spring. Wary of the West yet open to European social democracy and the Italian communists, they draw on academics, editors, old Bolsheviks and the readers of Novy Mir.

4.name: Kommunisticheskaya partiya Sovetskogo Soyuza
4.english: Communist Party of the Soviet Union
4.text:
The Communist Party of the Soviet Union is the ruling and only legal party of the USSR, with some fourteen million members. Since Khrushchev's fall in October 1964 it has been led by Leonid Brezhnev, General Secretary since 1966, within a collective leadership including Premier Alexei Kosygin, head of state Nikolai Podgorny and chief ideologist Mikhail Suslov. It is preparing the Lenin centenary and its Twenty-Fourth Congress.

Brezhnev's course promises 'stability of cadres' to the nomenklatura, steady growth to consumers, nuclear parity with the United States and the Brezhnev Doctrine, sealed by the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968. Talks with Bonn and on strategic arms coexist with a tense frontier against China. Its leverage is absolute: apparatus, army, KGB and planned economy all answer to its Politburo.
4.wiki: Communist Party of the Soviet Union

5.name: Svobodnye sovety truda
5.text:
The Free Councils of Labour stand for the shop-floor radicals who remember Novocherkassk, where troops shot down striking workers in June 1962. Their leading figure is Pyotr Siuda, a young worker at the city's Electric Locomotive Plant who addressed the crowd, was sentenced to twelve years, freed in 1966 and is back at work. Around him are workers angered by raised norms, food prices and the privileges of the bosses.

Their programme is soviets without the party: elected factory councils, workers' control over norms and wages, independent unions and self-management instead of ministries. They distrust the West as much as the nomenklatura and quote Lenin's State and Revolution against both. Their leverage is small but explosive: the memory of riots from Temirtau to Murom and Novocherkassk.

6.name: Neostalinistskaya platforma
6.text:
The Neo-Stalinist Platform gathers the hardliners who want Stalin's name restored and the Thaw undone. Its leading figure is Sergei Trapeznikov, Brezhnev's associate from Moldavia and head of the Central Committee's Department of Science and Educational Institutions since 1965, who disciplines 'revisionist' historians and was humiliatingly voted down by the Academy of Sciences. Writers such as Vsevolod Kochetov, author of the 1969 novel 'What Is It You Want?', give it a voice.

It demands strict ideological discipline, an end to camp literature, a purge of Novy Mir, an economy mobilized for heavy industry and defence, and vigilance against the West, Zionism and China alike. It finds sympathy in the apparatus, the army's political administration and among veterans who toasted Stalin's ninetieth birthday in December 1969.

7.name: Komsomolskiy avangard
7.text:
The Komsomol Vanguard is the network of former youth league and KGB officials loyal to Alexander Shelepin, 'Iron Shurik': Komsomol chief from 1952, KGB chairman from 1958 and an organizer of Khrushchev's overthrow in 1964. Brezhnev has dismantled much of his clan, removing Vladimir Semichastny from the KGB and Nikolai Yegorychev from the Moscow party in 1967, and parked Shelepin at the head of the trade unions, yet he keeps his Politburo seat.

The 'komsomoltsy' offer order rather than reform: a strong leader, iron discipline, a purge of the corrupt and the idle, a harder line toward Washington and a policed society mobilized through youth brigades. Their leverage lies in former Komsomol cadres across the state, friends in the security organs and the vast trade-union machine.

8.name: Zakavkazskoye islamskoye vozrozhdeniye
8.text:
The Transcaucasian Islamic Revival is the clandestine voice of Azerbaijan's believing Shia, guided by a Shia Revival Council of unregistered mullahs and village elders. Only a handful of mosques remain open, yet families still mourn Imam Husayn in Muharram, visit the pirs, the saints' shrines of Absheron and Lankaran, and look across the Araxes to the clergy of Iran. Many revere Grand Ayatollah Shariatmadari of Qom, a native of Tabriz.

The council seeks freedom of worship rather than revolution: reopened mosques, religious schooling, legal pilgrimage to Mashhad and Karbala and respect for Shia customs within Soviet law. It rejects Western materialism and Soviet atheism alike. Its leverage lies in village networks, family piety and a Shia identity that fifty years of propaganda have not erased.

9.name: Strazhi very
9.text:
The Guardians of the Faith are the most radical of Azerbaijan's underground Shia, led by a secret Council of Guardians that admits only proven believers. Their circles meet in private homes in old Baku and in pious Absheron villages such as Nardaran, inspired by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled by the Shah and teaching in Najaf since 1965, whose words reach them only through rumour and the rare traveller from Iran.

They reject the Soviet order outright and dream of a state ruled by the clergy and the sharia, purged of atheism, alcohol and Russian customs, and hostile to both superpowers. Their leverage is tiny but zealous: fervent young men, illegal mullahs and tight-knit village clans that the KGB watches but has never fully penetrated.

10.name: Bukharskaya restavratsiya
10.text:
The Bukharan Restoration keeps alive the dream of the Emirate of Bukhara, abolished by the Red Army in 1920. Its last emir, Mohammed Alim Khan, died in exile in Kabul in 1944; his heirs and courtiers' families live on among the Bukharan émigrés of Afghanistan, Turkey and the Hejaz, where a Bukharan Regency Council claims to guard the rights of the Manghit dynasty until the throne can be restored.

It stands for a Muslim monarchy under the Hanafi sharia, with the ulama, merchants and landed families restored and the atheist state swept away. Sympathetic to Saudi Arabia and the Muslim World League, it has no foothold inside Uzbekistan beyond old men's memories and the reverence still paid to the shrines and madrasas of Bukhara.

11.name: Vozrozhdeniye basmachestva
11.text:
The Basmachi Revival calls up the ghosts of the Muslim guerrillas who fought Soviet power across Turkestan from 1918 into the 1930s under commanders such as Kurshirmat and Ibrahim Bek. A secret Ferghana Mujahideen Council links unregistered mullahs and their hujra students in the valley with fighters' sons among the Turkestani émigrés of northern Afghanistan, who still honour Enver Pasha, killed by the Red Army in 1922.

Its programme is holy war: the expulsion of Russian power and atheism from Central Asia and a single Islamic Turkestan ruled by the sharia under a caliph. It rejects communism and the West alike as infidel. Its leverage is minimal but persistent: illegal religious schooling, clan solidarity and resentment over cotton quotas and Russian settlers.

12.name: Musulmanskiye dukhovnye reformatory
12.text:
The Muslim Spiritual Reformists form around Ziyauddin Babakhanov, Mufti of the Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan in Tashkent since 1957, heir to his father Eshon Babakhan. Through the Mir-i Arab madrasa in Bukhara, the journal Muslims of the Soviet East and constant travel to the Arab world as an envoy of Soviet diplomacy, he is the public face of Islam in the USSR.

Babakhanov preaches a purified, scripture-based faith, issuing fatwas against shrine pilgrimage, costly rituals and folk superstition, while insisting that Islam and socialism can coexist. His reformists seek more mosques, trained imams and translated texts through loyalty, not confrontation. They back the Arab states against Israel, and their leverage lies in legal status and usefulness to Soviet diplomacy.

13.name: Tekhnokratiya Gosplana
13.text:
The Gosplan Technocracy is the power of the planners: the State Planning Committee, the branch ministries and the engineers who run them. Its leader is Nikolai Baibakov, an oil engineer who rose under Stalin as people's commissar for the oil industry and has chaired Gosplan again since 1965. He is drafting the Ninth Five-Year Plan for 1971 to 1975, built on the new oil of Western Siberia.

The technocrats care for balances, not slogans: material flows, investment priorities and output targets set by specialists, increasingly with computers. They distrust both market experiments and ideological campaigns and want the party to leave the economy to professionals. Neutral toward East and West, they will buy any technology that raises output. Their leverage is the plan itself, which decides every minister's fate.

14.name: Zhit ne po lzhi
14.text:
Live Not by Lies is the moral creed of Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn and the Christian-conservative intelligentsia around him: refuse to repeat the official lie. Expelled from the Writers' Union in November 1969, Solzhenitsyn lives at the dacha of the cellist Mstislav Rostropovich near Moscow, while The First Circle and Cancer Ward circulate in samizdat and Western editions. Village-prose writers such as Vasily Belov and Valentin Rasputin share much of his outlook.

Its vision is national and religious, not Western: an end to Marxist ideology, freedom for the Orthodox Church, revival of the ruined Russian village and the North, and a nation that turns inward instead of policing an empire. It accepts authority if honest and lawful, distrusts liberal capitalism and communism alike, and draws strength from moral prestige.

15.name: Krasnye direktora
15.text:
The Red Directors are the managers of the great Soviet enterprises, the trade bosses and the regional clans who quietly turn state property into personal fiefdoms. Their patron is Nikolai Shchelokov, Brezhnev's friend from Dnepropetrovsk and Moldavia and Minister of Internal Affairs since 1966, who is rebuilding the militia's prestige and shields useful men in the ministries, the trade networks and the shadow economy of underground workshops.

They want autonomy beyond Kosygin's 1965 reform: the right to keep profits, trade surplus output, choose suppliers and reward loyal staff, with the police looking the other way. Ideology interests them little, and the West is a welcome source of machinery and consumer goods. Their leverage is control of production and supply, black-market cash and protection reaching the General Secretary's circle.

16.name: Liga svobodnogo predprinimatelstva
16.text:
The Free Enterprise League is the boldest circle of Soviet reform economists, those who privately conclude that the plan cannot be fixed and that markets must replace it. Its leading figure is Nikolai Shmelyov, a young specialist on the world economy, flanked by admirers of Yevsei Liberman's profit debate and of Ivan Khudenko's self-financing work teams at Akchi in Kazakhstan, whose spectacular results the authorities are now trying to bury.

It wants free prices, a legal private sector in services, farming and crafts, profit as the measure of every enterprise and open trade with the West. Its natural base is everyone already living by the market: kolkhoz market sellers, private plot holders and freelance building crews. Its leverage is intellectual and hidden, since such ideas cannot be printed.

17.name: Druzya Baykala
17.text:
The Friends of Baikal are the scientists, writers and students who have made the world's deepest lake the first great environmental cause of the Soviet Union. Their leading figure is the limnologist Grigory Galazy, director of the Limnological Institute at Irkutsk, who has fought the Baikalsk pulp and paper mill since before its effluent began reaching the lake in 1966. Academicians, the writer Vladimir Chivilikhin and Komsomolskaya Pravda back the cause.

They want strict limits on industrial pollution, new nature reserves and protection of forests and rivers from gigantomania, including schemes to turn Siberian rivers southwards. Patriots of the Russian land rather than enemies of the system, they rely on scientific authority, the press and public sympathy, already reflected in a government decree protecting Baikal in January 1969.

18.name: Sotsialisticheskoye rynochnoye sodruzhestvo
18.text:
The Socialist Market Commonwealth gathers the reform communists who look to Budapest and Belgrade rather than to Washington. Its leading figure is Alexander Yakovlev, a war veteran, former exchange student at Columbia University and acting head of the Central Committee's Propaganda Department, who hides his doubts behind the party line. Around him are economists of the Central Economic Mathematical Institute and the Novosibirsk school who defended Kosygin's 1965 reform.

They want socialism with a market: self-financing enterprises, prices set partly by supply and demand, workers' councils and room for small private trade, as in Hungary's New Economic Mechanism and Yugoslav self-management. They favour detente, trade with both blocs and a looser alliance in Eastern Europe. Their leverage rests on institutes, editors and officials frustrated by the reform's retreat.

19.name: Soyuz suverennykh respublik
19.text:
The Union of Sovereign Republics is the alliance of republican party leaders who want the Soviet Union to be a real federation. Its leading figure is Pyotr Shelest, First Secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine since 1963 and a full Politburo member, who defends Ukrainian industry against Moscow's ministries, promotes Ukrainian history and language and has written a hymn to his republic, 'O Ukraine, Our Soviet Land'.

Hard on dissidents and a hawk on Prague in 1968, Shelest is no liberal. His camp wants sovereignty for each republic within socialism: control over its own budget, industry and schools, protection of national languages against Russification and a looser union of equal Soviet states. Suspicious of America and of detente, it draws strength from republican apparatuses and Ukraine's economic weight.

20.name: Russkaya partiya
20.text:
The Russian Party is the informal nationalist lobby inside the Soviet establishment. Its patron in the Politburo is Dmitry Polyansky, First Deputy Premier and former head of the Russian Federation's government. Its voice is the Komsomol journal Molodaya Gvardiya, defended in 1969 by eleven writers in Ogonyok against Novy Mir, and its milieu includes the monument preservation society, the painter Ilya Glazunov and the admirers of village prose.

It puts Russia before the empire and world revolution: no more subsidies for the other republics and distant allies, restored churches and monuments, pride in Russian history from the tsars to Stalin's victory and a struggle against 'cosmopolitanism' and Zionism. Hostile to Western culture and liberal dissidents, it holds sway in Komsomol publishing, parts of the army and the Russian apparatus.

21.name: Komitet natsionalnogo vozrozhdeniya
21.text:
The Committee of National Rebirth is the hidden ultranationalist underground, run by a collective leadership that keeps no records and names no chief. It gathers the debris of circles the KGB has already broken, above all the antisemitic group of Alexander Fetisov, rounded up in 1968, and recruits among embittered veterans, disgraced officials and young men passing forbidden émigré pamphlets from hand to hand.

It wants a dictatorship of national rebirth: a Russian state cleansed of 'alien' influence, a purge of the party and the intelligentsia, a nation defined by blood, autarky and isolation from both the West and the 'internationalist' empire. Its leverage is small but dangerous: secrecy, sympathizers on the fringes of the Russian Party and the hope that a crisis will open the door.

22.name: Sovet marshalov
22.text:
The Council of Marshals is the high command of the Soviet Armed Forces as a political force. Its leading figure is Marshal Andrei Grechko, Minister of Defence since 1967, an army commander of the war who later led the forces of the Warsaw Pact. Around him stand Marshal Matvei Zakharov, Chief of the General Staff, Admiral of the Fleet Sergei Gorshkov, builder of an ocean-going navy.

The marshals want an army second to none: parity and then superiority over the United States, a fortified frontier with China after the Ussuri clashes of 1969, a firm grip on Eastern Europe and an unquestioned defence budget. Their leverage is immense: millions of men under arms, the nuclear arsenal and a decisive voice in the economy.

23.name: Dom Romanovykh
23.text:
The House of Romanov, which ruled Russia from 1613 to 1917, is represented by Grand Duke Vladimir Kirillovich, head of the imperial house since 1938 and son of the self-proclaimed emperor-in-exile Kirill. He lives in Madrid and Brittany with his wife, Princess Leonida Bagration-Mukhranskaya, and their only child, Maria. Other Romanov princes dispute his authority and reject his 1969 act securing the succession for his daughter.

The monarchists dream of a restored Orthodox empire, constitutional or autocratic, and an end to communism. They enjoy the sympathy of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia and of the Russian Imperial Union-Order, but have no organization inside the Soviet Union. Their leverage is symbolic: a historic name and a dynasty still remembered in Russian villages.
